Physiology of Digestion and Absorption
• Aging and the digestive system
• GI tract activity declines with age
• produces less digestive juice;
• absorption is less efficient;
• peristalsis slows, causing decline in frequency of bowel movements
• Taste/smell becomes less acute; periodontal disease often develops
• Constipation, fecal incontinence, and cancer of GI tract are fairly common
• Prevention: regular dental and medical examinations

summary_units.title: Overview of the digestive system
summary_units.summary: Overview of Digestive System • A healthy digestive system is essential to maintain life because it converts foods into raw materials that build and fuel our cells. • Main functions of the digestive system • Ingestion • Digestion • Absorption Absorb molecules into the bloodstream • Egestion Rid body of any indigestible remains Overview of Digestive System • Organs of the digestive system fall into two groups: • (1) Alimentary canal (gastrointestinal or GI tract or gut • (2) Accessory digestive organs Overview of Digestive System • (1) Alimentary canal • Continuous muscular tube • From the mouth to anus • Peristalsis • Site of digesting food breaks down food into smaller molecules • Absorbs food molecules into blood/lymph • Organs • mouth • Stomach • small intestine • large intestine Overview of Digestive System • (2) Accessory digestive organs • Teeth • Tongue • Gallbladder • Digestive glands produce secretions that help break down food chemically • Salivary glands • Liver • Pancreas

summary_units.summary: Anatomy of Digestive System • Mouth and Associated Organs • Mouth (Oral cavity / Buccal cavity) is where food is ingested, chewed, and mixed with saliva that begins process of digestion, and swallowing process is initiated • Associated organs include: • Tongue • Salivary glands • Teeth Name of Muscle Description Origin (O) Insertion (I) Action Muscles of Mastication (Self-Study Closes off nasopharynx during swallowing Teeth: Chewing to tear and grind food into smaller fragments 20 milk teeth 32 permanent teeth Gripping, positioning, and mixing of food during chewing Mixing food and saliva to form bolus Involving in swallowing, speech, and taste Closes off trachea during swallowing Functions of saliva ➢ Cleanses mouth ➢ Dissolves food chemicals for taste ➢ Moistens food; compacts into bolus ➢ Begins breakdown of starch with enzyme salivary amylase Anything that inhibits saliva secretion can promote tooth decay Lack of saliva also makes it difficult to talk and swallow Anatomy of Digestive System • Pharynx • Connects to esophagus and trachea • Allows passage of food, fluids, and air • Esophagus • Muscular tube that runs from pharynx to stomach • Peristalsis for squeezing bolus toward stomach • Secrete mucus to enhance bolus movement • Heartburn Discomfort burning sensation caused by stomach acid regurgitating into esophagus

summary_units.title: Physiology of digestion and absorption
summary_units.summary: Physiology of Digestion and Absorption • Chemical Digestion • Breaks down ingested foods into their chemical building blocks • Digestive enzymes are involved • Final end products are small enough to be absorbed across wall of small intestine • Absorption • Moves substances from lumen of gut into body • Most nutrients are absorbed before chyme reaches ileum • Passive and active ways of membrane transport are use Physiology of Digestion and Absorption • Digestive juices in small intestine • Bile • Produce by liver; Store by gallbladder; Release into duodenum • Contains bile acid and phospholipids for emulsifying lipids • Contains bicarbonate for neutralizing gastric acid • Other components: bile pigment, cholesterols, ions ○ Pancreatic juice • Produce by pancreas; Release into duodenum • Contains digestive enzymes for chemical digestion of carbohydrate, proteins, and lipids • Contains bicarbonate for neutralizing gastric acid Physiology of Digestion and Absorption Monosaccharides are absorbed into blood via facilitated diffusion and secondary active transport! Amino acids are absorbed into blood via facilitated diffusion and secondary active transport!

• Main functions of the digestive system
• Absorption Absorb molecules into the bloodstream
• Egestion Rid body of any indigestible remains
• Organs of the digestive system fall into two groups:
• (1) Alimentary canal (gastrointestinal or GI tract or gut
• (2) Accessory digestive organs
• Site of digesting food breaks down food into smaller molecules
• Absorbs food molecules into blood/lymph
• (2) Accessory digestive organs

• The processing of food by the digestive system involves 6 activities:
• (1) Ingestion eating, taking food via the mouth
• (2) Propulsion movement of food from mouth to anus
• The processing of food by the digestive system involves 6 activities:
• (3) Mechanical digestion physically breaking food into small pieces for chemical digestion
• Mixing food with digestive juice
• (4) Chemical digestion catabolic reactions enhanced by enzymes
• break down complex food molecules into simple chemical building blocks
• The processing of food by the digestive system involves 6 activities:
• (5) Absorption passage of digested molecules from lumen of GI tract into blood or lymph
• (6) Defecation elimination of indigestible substances via anus in form of feces
Basic Structure of Alimentary Canal
• Walls of alimentary canal have the same four basic tissue layers
• Epithelium that covers surface of lumen
• Secretes mucus, digestive enzymes, and hormones
• Absorbs end products of digestion
• Protects against infectious disease
• Contains blood and lymphatic vessels, and nerve plexus
• Inner circular layer and outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle tissue for peristalsis

• Major functions of large intestine is propulsion of feces to anus and defecation

• Digestive enzymes are involved
• Final end products are small enough to be absorbed across wall of small intestine
• Moves substances from lumen of gut into body
• Most nutrients are absorbed before chyme reaches ileum
• Passive and active ways of membrane transport are use
• Digestive juices in small intestine
• Produce by liver; Store by gallbladder; Release into duodenum
• Contains bile acid and phospholipids for emulsifying lipids
• Contains bicarbonate for neutralizing gastric acid
• Other components: bile pigment, cholesterols, ions

• In rare cases, intact proteins are taken up by intestinal epithelial cells by endocytosis and are released into body
• More common in patients with immature/weak intestinal mucosa such as newborn infants
• May result in food allergies as immune system “sees” intact proteins as harmful and starts an attack
• Allergies usually disappear as mucosa matures
• Digestion and Absorption of Lipids
• Digestion of lipids occurs mainly in small intestine.
• Bile is essential for lipid emulsification.
• Lipase in pancreatic juice is essential for chemical digestion of triglyceride.
• 9 L water enter small intestine everyday
• Over 80% is absorbed in the small intestine by osmosis
• Most of rest is absorbed in large intestine
• Net osmosis occurs when difference of water potentials is made by active transport of solutes (Mainly Na + )
• →Water uptake is coupled with solute uptake
• Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) are carried by micelles and absorbed by simple diffusion
• Water-soluble vitamins (C and B) are absorbed by facilitated diffusion or active transport
• Vitamin B12 (large molecule) binds with intrinsic factor and is absorbed by endocytosis
• vitamin K and B vitamins made by friendly bacteria are absorbed
• Iron and calcium are absorbed in duodenum
• Iron and calcium absorption is related to need
• Iron ions are stored in mucosal cells. When needed, the ions are transported in blood
• Ca absorption is regulated by vitamin D and parathyroid hormone (PTH)
• Regulation of Digestive Secretion
• Secretion of digestive juices is controlled by both nervous activities and hormones.
• Generally stimulated by parasympathetic division and inhibited by sympathetic division of autonomic nervous system (ANS)
• Endocrine (hormonal) regulation
• Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP)
• Aging and the digestive system
• GI tract activity declines with age
• produces less digestive juice;
• peristalsis slows, causing decline in frequency of bowel movements
• Taste/smell becomes less acute; periodontal disease often develops
• Constipation, fecal incontinence, and cancer of GI tract are fairly common
• Prevention: regular dental and medical examinations
